name: PCA9306DQER
title: PCA9306: two-channel bidirectional level translator for I2C and SMBus
summary: A two-channel pass-switch translator for SCL and SDA that joins an I2C or SMBus segment on a 1.2 V to 3.3 V reference (VREF1) to one on 1.8 V to 5.5 V (VREF2), with no direction pin. Each channel is an N-channel switch of a few ohms whose gate bias is set by a resistor-fed reference transistor; EN low isolates the two sides. Also used to cut off a slower bus segment or to hot-insert a board. Offered in SSOP, VSSOP, X2SON and DSBGA; PCA9306DQER is the 1.4 mm x 1 mm X2SON on a 5000-piece reel.
key_figures: 3.5 Ω typ at EN = 4.5 V, IO = 64 mA
standard-mode and fast-mode I2C (400 kHz); bandwidth above 100 MHz
64 mA max recommended; 128 mA continuous absolute max
5 V tolerant; high-impedance with EN low

circuits.title: Simplified application
circuits.description: A controller on the low-voltage side talks to target devices on the high-voltage side. VREF1 takes the low-side supply; VREF2 and EN are joined and fed from the high-side pull-up supply through 200 kΩ, so the switch is on whenever that supply is up.

circuits.title: Normal setup, 1.8 V to 3.3 V
circuits.description: The usual translator wiring: VREF1 on the 1.8 V rail, VREF2 tied to EN and pulled to 3.3 V through 200 kΩ. EN settles at 1.8 V plus the pass-FET threshold, with about 4 µA flowing into VREF2. Each of the four bus lines has its own pull-up to its own side's rail.
notes: IREF2 = 4 µA; EN = +1.8 V + VTH.

circuits.title: Switch configuration, VREF1 = VREF2
circuits.description: Both sides run from one supply level, so the part acts as a bus switch rather than a translator. VREF1 sits on VCC1, VREF2 is pulled to VCC2 (equal to VCC1) through 200 kΩ, and EN is driven separately by a GPIO whose high level stays at or below VREF2 + Vth.
notes: GPIO high level not above Vref2 + Vth.

circuits.title: Translation configuration
circuits.description: VREF1 on the low rail VCC1; VREF2 and EN joined and pulled up to VCC2 through 200 kΩ, with VCC2 at least VREF1 + 0.7 V. Each bus line is pulled up to the rail of its own side.
notes: VCC2 ≥ VREF1 + 0.7 V.

circuits.title: Controller on side 2
circuits.description: The same translator wiring with the roles swapped: the controller sits on the SCL2/SDA2 side and the targets on the SCL1/SDA1 side. VREF2 and EN are joined and pulled to VCC2 through 200 kΩ; VREF1 is on VCC1.

circuits.title: VREF1 from an LDO, with a bias-current pull-down
circuits.description: VREF1 is powered by a 1.8 V LDO. The bias current that flows from VREF2 into VREF1 has a path to ground through Rpulldown, so the LDO, which cannot sink it, keeps regulation. CREF1 sits on the VREF1 node; VREF2 and EN are joined and pulled to 3.3 V through 200 kΩ.

notes: Ibias = (Vcc2 – Ven) / 200 k; Ven = Vref1 + VTH.

circuits.title: Typical application, switch always enabled
circuits.description: A 1.8 V I2C controller connected to a 3.3 V I2C device. VREF1 is on the 1.8 V rail, which also powers the controller. VREF2 and EN are joined, bypassed by a capacitor to ground and pulled to VDPU = 3.3 V through 200 kΩ, so the switch is on whenever VDPU is present. RPU pull-ups take SCL1 and SDA1 to 1.8 V and SCL2 and SDA2 to 3.3 V; VDPU also powers the device.
notes: RPU from the pull-up resistance curves.
200 kΩ is the typical value.

circuits.title: Typical application, switch enable control
circuits.description: The same 1.8 V controller to 3.3 V device link, but the 200 kΩ resistor to the joined VREF2 and EN pins is fed by a 3.3 V enable signal instead of VDPU. With the signal high the switch conducts; with it low the two buses are disconnected. The pull-ups still go to 1.8 V and to VDPU = 3.3 V.
notes: Enable signal: off low, on at 3.3 V.

operation.text: Two identical N-channel pass switches, one for SCL and one for SDA, whose gates share the EN pin. A third, matching reference transistor between VREF1 and VREF2 sets the gate bias. The two channels are matched, so their voltages and delays track closely. There is no direction pin; either side may drive.

VREF1 runs from 1.2 V to 3.3 V and VREF2 from 1.8 V to 5.5 V. Supported pairs: 1.2 V VREF1 with 1.8, 2.5, 3.3 or 5 V VREF2; 1.8 V with 2.5, 3.3 or 5 V; 2.5 V with 3.3 or 5 V; 3.3 V with 5 V. The bus pins tolerate 5 V.
Vth, the threshold of the NFET between VREF1 and VREF2, is about 0.6 V at room temperature.

For translation, EN and VREF2 are shorted and pulled to the high-side supply through a high-value resistor, typically 200 kΩ. The node settles at VREF1 + Vth, which lets lows pass between the sides while each side keeps its own pull-up voltage. VREF1 may connect straight to its supply; leaving out the high-value resistor between VREF2 and VDPU draws excessive current and makes operation unreliable. Tying VREF2 straight to the high rail with no resistor leaves nothing to limit the current from VCC2 into VCC1 once VCC2 exceeds VCC1 by Vth; the current can then exceed the 128 mA continuous channel rating and destroy the pass FET, and grows with the difference between the rails.

EN high turns both switches on: SCL1 joins SCL2 and SDA1 joins SDA2. EN low turns them off and leaves all four bus pins high-impedance, without lockup. A channel conducts while EN is 0.6 V or more above its side-1 or side-2 pin. With EN tied to VREF2 the part is on whenever VREF2 has power; a processor signal driving the 200 kΩ resistor turns it on and off.

When either pin of a channel is pulled low, the switch conducts and the other side follows low through a few ohms. When both sides are released, the low side rises to its own pull-up rail, limited to the level set by VREF1, and the switch turns off; the high side is then pulled to VDPU by its own resistors. Each side needs its own pull-up resistors.

A push-pull or an open-drain controller output works; the device side is open-drain with pull-ups to VDPU. A push-pull driver on either side means one-way traffic, or three-state drivers steered by some direction logic so that highs and lows never fight. Two open-drain sides need no direction logic at all.
The 400 pF I2C load limit covers side 1 and side 2 together.

The part can split a bus into a faster and a slower segment: EN is taken low to cut off a 100 kHz (or 400 kHz) segment while the main bus runs at 400 kHz (or 1 MHz), and brought high only when traffic across both segments runs at the slower rate. With a 400 kHz controller the overall bus rate may fall below 400 kHz because of the added delay. The GPIO that drives EN must not go above 3.3 V + Vth in the 3.3 V example.

For a remote board plugged into a backplane bus, the part is held disabled during insertion and turned on after the remote board has power and both buses are idle, so no glitch on SCL can corrupt a transfer or hang a device.

With VREF1 equal to VREF2 the part acts as a plain bus switch, EN driven by a GPIO whose high stays at or below VREF2 + Vth. In this mode, with equal pull-ups and loads, delay is the same in both directions, and shorter at higher supply (longer at 1.8 V than at 5 V). In translation mode, lows pass from side 1 to side 2 faster than from side 2 to side 1, and the gap widens as VCC2 - VCC1 grows.
Signals pass both ways, so the controller may sit on side 1 or on side 2.

The bias current flows from VREF2 into VREF1. An LDO that cannot sink it lets the VREF1 node charge up until the pass-FET Vgs equals Vth, leaving VREF1 at VCC2 - Vth, which can overstress parts powered from that LDO. A resistor from VREF1 to ground, sized by the pull-down equations, gives the current a path.
The 200 kΩ resistor may be made smaller; the bias current rises in proportion, and the resistor must stay large enough that the current stays under the 128 mA continuous channel rating.
A 100 pF capacitor on VREF2 is recommended, placed as close to the pin as possible. A larger capacitor also works but its time constant with the 200 kΩ resistor lengthens turn-on and turn-off.
The pull-up resistance curves give the largest and smallest values the I2C rules allow at 100 kHz (standard mode) and 400 kHz (fast mode). Standard-mode I2C devices specify only 3 mA sink current.

The channel's top frequency depends on loading; above 100 MHz is reachable in the right conditions. The part has no drive of its own, unlike buffered repeaters, so fast signals need a strong host driver; with a push-pull CMOS host no host-side pull-up is needed. A rule of thumb is a bandwidth of five times the clock rate. For best results: keep the part close to the processor's I2C output, keep trace length below half the flight time to avoid ringing and reflections, keep the sink-side (1.8 V) trace short, and add a pull-up on the 1.8 V side to cut overshoot at the cost of a slower fall.

I2C speeds need no controlled impedance or differential routing. Avoid right-angle traces, fan traces apart leaving the chip, and widen power and ground traces. Two layers can work, signals on top and a split power/ground plane below; four layers suit denser routing, with inner ground and power planes and vias right beside the supply and ground pads. The DQE package needs a board thermal pad under it.
